alt: The set seen fills with 3 and 5, and a second add of 3 is rejected because a set never stores a duplicate. The set unique then builds the same way from a line of numbers read from input, one duplicate token at a time being rejected, ending sorted.

steps.caption: `seen = set()` starts empty, then `seen.add(3)` inserts 3.
Adding 3 again does nothing. A set never stores the same value twice, so `seen` still holds only one 3.
`seen.add(5)` inserts 5. `seen` now holds 3 and 5.
`len(seen)` is 2, not 3: the second `add(3)` never grew the set.
`3 in seen` is True, checked the same way as `in` on a dict's keys.
The comprehension reads 2 and adds it to `unique`.
The next token is 2 again. Adding a duplicate to a set changes nothing, so `unique` still holds [2].
The comprehension reads 3 and adds it to `unique`.
The comprehension reads 4 and adds it to `unique`.
The next token is 3 again. Adding a duplicate to a set changes nothing, so `unique` still holds [2, 3, 4].
`sorted(unique)` prints [2, 3, 4]: every duplicate token collapsed into the one value already there.
